<problem>
Let
\[
F=(f_1,f_2,f_3)=(y,zy-x^2,z^2+x^2y+zy^2+x^3),\qquad f=f_1f_2f_3.
\]
Consider the parameter hyperplane
\[
H=\{(s_1,s_2,s_3)\in\mathbb C^3:2s_1+6s_2+8s_3+27=0\}.
\]
For \(s\in H\), write \(\beta=s_2+1\) and \(\gamma=s_3+1\). Let \(U\subset H\) consist of the parameters satisfying
\[
\beta,\ \gamma,\ \beta+\gamma+\tfrac32,\ \beta+2\gamma+\tfrac32,\ 2(\beta+\gamma+1)\notin\mathbb Z.
\]

Let \(a,c\) be independent indeterminates, put
\[
Q_2=c-a^{-1},\qquad Q_3=c^2+c+a^{-1},
\]
and define the localization
\[
R=\mathbb C[a,a^{-1},c,c^{-1},Q_2^{-1},Q_3^{-1},(c+a^{-1})^{-1}].
\]
Write \(\Omega_R^j\) for the algebraic differential \(j\)-forms over \(\mathbb C\), with exterior differential \(d\). For each \(s\in U\), set
\[
\theta_s=-\frac{27}{2}\frac{da}{a}+s_2\frac{dQ_2}{Q_2}+s_3\frac{dQ_3}{Q_3},
\qquad
\mathcal H_s=\frac{\Omega_R^2}{\{d\eta+\theta_s\wedge\eta:\eta\in\Omega_R^1\}},
\]
where the quotient is taken as a complex vector space.

For an independent formal variable \(b\), define a complex-linear map \(J_s:\mathbb C[x,y,z]\to\mathcal H_s\) by
\[
J_s(\psi)=\left[-a^3[b^{18}]\left(\psi(ab^3,ab^2,a^2b^4c)\left(1+\frac{a^{-1}b}{Q_3}\right)^{s_3}\right)\,da\wedge dc\right].
\]
Here \([b^{18}]\) denotes coefficient extraction in \(R[[b]]\), the outer brackets denote the class in \(\mathcal H_s\), and formal powers are interpreted by
\[
(1+T)^{s_3}=\sum_{n\ge0}\frac{s_3(s_3-1)\cdots(s_3-n+1)}{n!}T^n,
\]
with empty product equal to \(1\). Define
\[
W_s=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb C}\{J_s(f\psi):\psi\in\mathbb C[x,y,z]\}\subseteq\mathcal H_s.
\]
Let \(\mathcal E\) be the Zariski closure in \(\mathbb C^3\) of
\[
\{s\in U:W_s\ne\mathcal H_s\}.
\]
What is the reduced Gröbner basis of the vanishing ideal \(I(\mathcal E)\subset\mathbb C[s_1,s_2,s_3]\) for the lexicographic monomial order \(s_1\succ s_2\succ s_3\)?
</problem>

11	We prove this by identifying \(\mathcal H_s\) with a tensor product of two one-variable twisted de Rham quotients. In these coordinates, the two generators of \(W_s\) admit explicit reductions.
12	
13	## 1. The two possible generators of \(W_s\)
14	
15	Throughout, write
16	\[
17	B=\beta=s_2+1,\qquad G=\gamma=s_3+1.
18	\]
19	Under the substitution in the definition of \(J_s\),
20	\[
21	f(ab^3,ab^2,a^2b^4c)
22	=a^8b^{16}Q_2Q_3\left(1+\frac{a^{-1}b}{Q_3}\right).
23	\]
24	The weights of \(x,y,z\) are respectively \(3,2,4\). Thus a monomial \(\psi\) can contribute to \(J_s(f\psi)\) only if its weight is at most \(2\). The only such monomials are \(1,y\). Consequently,
25	\[
26	W_s=\operatorname{span}\{J_s(f),J_s(fy)\}.
27	\]
28	Coefficient extraction gives
29	\[
30	\begin{aligned}
31	J_s(f)&=\left[-\frac{G(G-1)}2a^9\frac{Q_2}{Q_3}\,da\wedge dc\right],\\
32	J_s(fy)&=\left[-a^{12}Q_2Q_3\,da\wedge dc\right].
33	\end{aligned}
34	\tag{1}
35	\]
36	
37	## 2. Coordinates separating the connection
38	
39	Put
40	\[
41	t=a^{-1},\qquad P=c-t,\qquad Q=c^2+c+t.
42	\]
43	The original connection form becomes
44	\[
45	\theta=\frac{27}{2}\frac{dt}{t}
46	 +(B-1)\frac{dP}{P}+(G-1)\frac{dQ}{Q}.
47	\]
48	For an invertible element \(g\), division of forms by \(g\) identifies the connection \(\theta\) with \(\theta+d\log g\). Take
49	\[
50	g=t^{-14}PQ.
51	\]
52	The new connection is
53	\[
54	\theta'=-\frac12\frac{dt}{t}+B\frac{dP}{P}+G\frac{dQ}{Q}.
55	\]
56	Since \(da=-t^{-2}dt\), the two classes in (1), after this identification, are
57	\[
58	[dt\wedge dc],\qquad
59	\frac{G(G-1)}2\left[\frac{t^3}{Q^2}\,dt\wedge dc\right],
60	\tag{2}
61	\]
62	in the order \(J_s(fy),J_s(f)\).
63	
64	Now set
65	\[
66	u=\frac tc,\qquad v=\frac{c^2}{c+t}.
67	\]
68	Their inverse formulas are
69	\[
70	c=(1+u)v,\qquad t=u(1+u)v.
71	\]
72	In particular,
73	\[
74	\begin{aligned}
75	P&=(1-u)(1+u)v,\\
76	Q&=(1+u)^2v(v+1),\\
77	c+t&=(1+u)^2v,\\
78	dt\wedge dc&=(1+u)^2v\,du\wedge dv.
79	\end{aligned}
80	\tag{3}
81	\]
82	These formulas identify the ring \(R\) with
83	\[
84	A_u\otimes_{\mathbb C}A_v,
85	\]
86	where
87	\[
88	\begin{aligned}
89	A_u&=\mathbb C[u,u^{-1},(u-1)^{-1},(u+1)^{-1}],\\
90	A_v&=\mathbb C[v,v^{-1},(v+1)^{-1}].
91	\end{aligned}
92	\]
93	
94	Apply one more gauge identification, dividing by the Jacobian
95	\[
96	h=(1+u)^2v.
97	\]
98	Define
99	\[
100	C=B+2G+\frac32,\qquad D=B+G+\frac12.
101	\]
102	The resulting connection separates:
103	\[
104	\omega=\omega_u+\omega_v,
105	\]
106	with
107	\[
108	\omega_u=-\frac12\frac{du}{u}
109	 +B\frac{du}{u-1}+C\frac{du}{u+1},
110	\qquad
111	\omega_v=D\frac{dv}{v}+G\frac{dv}{v+1}.
112	\tag{4}
113	\]
114	The generators (2) become
115	\[
116	[du\wedge dv],\qquad
117	\frac{G(G-1)}2
118	\left[\frac{u^3}{u+1}\frac{v}{(v+1)^2}\,du\wedge dv\right].
119	\tag{5}
120	\]
121	
122	## 3. The dimensions and bases, valid for every \(s\in U\)
123	
124	We use the following elementary reduction fact.
125	
126	**One-variable reduction lemma.** Let
127	\[
128	A=\mathbb C[z,(z-r_1)^{-1},\ldots,(z-r_m)^{-1}],\qquad
129	L=\frac d{dz}+\sum_{i=1}^m\frac{\lambda_i}{z-r_i}.
130	\]
131	If every \(\lambda_i\) and also \(\Lambda=\sum_i\lambda_i\) is nonintegral, then
132	\[
133	A/L(A)
134	\]
135	has basis \(1,z,\ldots,z^{m-2}\).
136	
137	Indeed, a pole of order \(k\ge2\) can be eliminated using \(L((z-r_i)^{-(k-1)})\), whose leading coefficient at that pole is
138	\(\lambda_i-(k-1)\ne0\). Simple poles can then be eliminated using polynomial interpolation and \(\lambda_i\ne0\).
139	
140	Conversely, if \(L(h)\) is polynomial, the same leading-pole argument shows that \(h\) is polynomial. Absence of simple poles then forces
141	\[
142	h=\prod_i(z-r_i)\,q(z).
143	\]
144	For \(q\) of degree \(n\), its image has degree \(n+m-1\), with leading coefficient multiplied by
145	\[
146	n+m+\Lambda\ne0.
147	\]
148	Thus precisely the asserted polynomial basis remains.
149	
150	Apply the lemma to (4). For the \(u\)-connection the residues are
151	\[
152	-\frac12,\ B,\ C,
153	\]
154	whose sum is
155	\[
156	S:=2B+2G+1.
157	\]
158	For the \(v\)-connection they are \(D,G\), whose sum is \(C-1\).
159	
160	Every required nonintegrality follows from the definition of \(U\):
161	\[
162	B,\ G,\ D,\ C,\ S\notin\mathbb Z.
163	\]
164	Therefore the one-variable quotients have bases
165	\[
166	\{[du],[u\,du]\},\qquad \{[dv]\},
167	\]
168	respectively.
169	
170	The top-degree quotient of the separated complex is their tensor product: explicitly, its relations are
171	\[
172	L_u(A_u)\otimes A_v+A_u\otimes L_v(A_v).
173	\]
174	Hence
175	\[
176	\dim_{\mathbb C}\mathcal H_s=2
177	\]
178	for every \(s\in U\), with basis represented in the final coordinates by
179	\[
180	du\wedge dv,\qquad u\,du\wedge dv.
181	\tag{6}
182	\]
183	
184	## 4. Exact reductions of the generators
185	
186	Write
187	\[
188	L_u=\frac d{du}-\frac1{2u}+\frac B{u-1}+\frac C{u+1},
189	\qquad
190	L_v=\frac d{dv}+\frac Dv+\frac G{v+1}.
191	\]
192	
193	First, in the \(v\)-quotient,
194	\[
195	\left[\frac{v}{(v+1)^2}\right]=K[1],
196	\qquad
197	K=-\frac{(D+1)(D+G+1)}{G(G-1)}.
198	\tag{7}
199	\]
200	An explicit exactness certificate is
201	\[
202	\frac{v}{(v+1)^2}-K
203	=L_v\left(
204	\frac{\displaystyle\frac v{v+1}+\frac{D+1}{G}v}{G-1}
205	\right).
206	\]
207	All denominators here are nonzero on \(U\).
208	
209	For the \(u\)-reduction, let \(P_u=u(u-1)(u+1)\). Direct differentiation gives
210	\[
211	\begin{aligned}
212	L_u(P_u)&=(S+3)u^2+(B-C)u-\frac12,\\
213	L_u(u(u-1))&=(S+2)u-\frac12-2C+\frac{2C}{u+1}.
214	\end{aligned}
215	\]
216	It follows that
217	\[
218	\left[\frac{u^3}{u+1}\right]=A_0[1]+A_1[u],
219	\tag{8}
220	\]
221	where
222	\[
223	A_0=\frac1{2(S+3)}-\frac1{4C},
224	\qquad
225	A_1=\frac{C-B}{S+3}-\frac GC.
226	\]
227	More explicitly,
228	\[
229	\frac{u^3}{u+1}-A_0-A_1u
230	=L_u\left(\frac{P_u}{S+3}-\frac{u(u-1)}{2C}\right).
231	\]
232	The coefficient determining linear independence is
233	\[
234	A_1=
235	\frac{6B+8G^2+8G+9}{4C(S+3)}.
236	\tag{9}
237	\]
238	
239	Relative to (6), the columns of the two generators in (5) form the matrix
240	\[
241	M=
242	\begin{pmatrix}
243	1&\dfrac{G(G-1)}2KA_0\\[2mm]
244	0&\dfrac{G(G-1)}2KA_1
245	\end{pmatrix}.
246	\]
247	Since \(D+G+1=C\), its determinant simplifies to
248	\[
249	\det M
250	=-\frac{(D+1)(6B+8G^2+8G+9)}{8(S+3)}.
251	\tag{10}
252	\]
253	On \(U\), both \(D+1\) and \(S+3\) are nonzero. We have therefore proved the exact, pointwise equivalence
254	\[
255	\boxed{\quad
256	W_s\ne\mathcal H_s
257	\iff
258	6\beta+8\gamma^2+8\gamma+9=0,
259	\qquad s\in U.
260	\quad}
261	\tag{11}
262	\]
263	
264	## 5. Closure and reduced Gröbner basis
265	
266	In the original parameters, the polynomial in (11) is
267	\[
268	N=6s_2+8s_3^2+24s_3+31.
269	\]
270	Thus the exceptional parameters in \(U\) lie on the curve
271	\[
272	2s_1+6s_2+8s_3+27=0,\qquad N=0.
273	\tag{12}
274	\]
275	
276	They are Zariski dense in this curve. To see this, parametrize it by \(G=\gamma\), with
277	\[
278	B=-\frac{8G^2+8G+9}{6}.
279	\]
280	Each of
281	\[
282	B,\quad G,\quad B+G+\frac32,\quad B+2G+\frac32,\quad 2(B+G+1)
283	\]
284	is then a nonconstant polynomial in \(G\) with rational coefficients. The excluded integrality conditions remove only countably many values of \(G\), so the remaining set is infinite and hence Zariski dense in this affine line.
285	
286	Consequently, \(\mathcal E\) is exactly the curve (12). Solving its equations gives
287	\[
288	s_2=-\frac43s_3^2-4s_3-\frac{31}{6},
289	\qquad
290	s_1=4s_3^2+8s_3+2.
291	\]
292	Its ideal is prime, since the coordinate ring is \(\mathbb C[s_3]\). The two displayed monic equations have leading monomials \(s_1,s_2\), and their tails involve only \(s_3\). They therefore constitute the reduced lexicographic Gröbner basis stated above.
